vignette: Elias sits across from me, his hands wrapped around a cooling mug of tea. At thirty-four, his face carries the early map of a life lived at high altitude. He grew up in a quiet town in northern Italy, where the concept of war felt like a subject in a textbook. He tells me about the deployment, how he signs up for the humanitarian relief contract after three years on the fire service roster. The mountains of northern Syria become his new beat. He remembers the dust, the constant hum of generators, the way the sky turns the color of bruised iron when the shelling starts. He doesn't go looking for combat, but combat finds him. One afternoon, a makeshift clinic collapses under direct fire. Elias digs through rubble with his bare hands, fingers bleeding, until he pulls out a child who will never draw breath again. That moment doesn't just happen to him; it lodges somewhere behind his ribs, heavy and immovable. He returns home to a quiet house in Ohio, to his wife, Clara, and the steady rhythm of suburban life. But the quiet feels thin, like paper stretched over a window. He starts working back on the fire department, wearing the same turnout gear, riding the same trucks. The first time the bell rings, his stomach drops as if it's already in the ground. He tries to shake it off, but the trigger sticks. Sirens don't just mean fire anymore; they mean the cadence of distant artillery. Smoke doesn't just smell of burning timber; it smells of cordite and wet plaster. When he climbs into the engine cab, his breath comes shallow, his palms slick against the steering wheel. He tells me he keeps replaying the collapse in his head when he tries to fall asleep. The images don't fade with the lights of his bedroom; they move closer, until he stops trying to sleep altogether. He has stopped sleeping on his side. Now he lies on his back, knees slightly drawn, one hand resting on the pillow beside him, waiting for a hand to grab that isn't there. Clara learns to wake without startling him. When she reaches for his shoulder, he flinches, then covers the flinch with a forced laugh. They haven't talked about it, but the distance between them in bed has widened into something physical and unspoken. He catches himself scanning every room they enter-exits, corners, the weight of a ceiling fan. At the grocery store, the sudden crash of a shopping cart makes him drop to one knee behind a produce display, heart hammering against his ribs. He gets up, straightens his coat, and walks out without buying the milk, telling himself he'll come back later, though he knows he won't. On shift, he pushes through the routine by clinging to procedure. He runs drills until his hands remember the movements without his brain interfering. He volunteers for the heavy extrication team, telling himself he needs to prove the old reflexes are still sharp. But when a call goes to a structural collapse, his throat tightens, and he has to step behind a pylon for thirty seconds just to regulate his breathing. He doesn't miss a beat on the scene-his voice stays level, his commands clear-but afterward, he sits in the decon bay, scrubbing dirt off his forearms until the water runs cold and the shaking starts. He tells me he misses the version of himself who used to joke in the mess hall, who used to forget the day by nine in the evening. Now, every evening is just a long exhale, waiting for the next alarm. He keeps his helmet on the passenger seat of his truck, not as a relic, but as an anchor. When the road gets too loud, he presses his palm against the smooth, scarred shell and waits for the world to stop spinning.
